content: A fume hood, also known as a fume cupboard, is a critical piece of laboratory equipment commonly found in chemistry labs. Its primary purpose is to minimize a user's exposure to hazardous or unpleasant fumes. Historically, fume hoods were constructed from timber, but modern units are typically made from epoxy-coated mild steel for enhanced durability and chemical resistance. There are two main types of fume hoods: ducted and recirculating. Ducted fume hoods expel air outside the building, while recirculating hoods filter the air and return it to the room. Older ducted systems that used asbestos vent pipes have been replaced with safer materials like PVC or polypropylene. Regardless of the type, the basic principle remains the same: air is drawn into the hood from the front via a fan, either expelled outside or filtered and recirculated. Construction and Location Fume hoods are available in various sizes, typically ranging in width from 1000 mm to 2000 mm, with depths between 700 mm and 900 mm, and heights from 1900 mm to 2400 mm. They can accommodate one to three operators and are usually installed against walls, often with infills above to conceal ductwork. Due to their design, the interior of fume hoods tends to be dimly lit, so many are equipped with internal lights protected by gas-proof covers. The front of the hood features a movable glass sash that can be adjusted vertically using a counterbalance mechanism. In educational settings, the sides of the hood are often made of glass to allow multiple students to observe experiments simultaneously. Many fume hoods also include alarm control panels for safety monitoring. Recirculating Fume Hoods Recirculating fume hoods are primarily used in educational settings or in buildings where external ductwork installation is not feasible. These units typically have a fan mounted on the top or beneath the work surface. Air is drawn in through the front opening, passed through a filter, and then recirculated back into the workspace. Pre-Filtration The first stage of filtration involves a physical barrier, often made of open-cell foam, which traps large particles. These pre-filters are inexpensive and generally last about six months, depending on usage. Main Filtration After pre-filtration, air passes through a layer of activated charcoal, which absorbs most chemical fumes. However, certain substances like ammonia and carbon monoxide can bypass standard carbon filters. Additional specialized filtration methods can be incorporated to address these chemicals. Main filters typically last around two years, depending on usage. Advantages of Recirculating Fume Hoods No external ductwork is required. Heated air is retained within the workspace, reducing energy loss. Contaminated air is not released into the atmosphere. Disadvantages of Recirculating Fume Hoods Filters require regular maintenance and replacement. There is a higher risk of chemical exposure compared to ducted systems. The proximity of the fan to the operator may result in increased noise levels. Ducted Fume Hoods Ducted fume hoods are the standard choice for industrial applications. These systems remove air from the workspace and expel it into the atmosphere. They are part of a larger laboratory ventilation system, which ensures that air from the lab is not recirculated into non-laboratory areas. Some labs use single-pass air handling systems, where air is used once before being discharged, to improve indoor air quality. However, many labs still employ return air systems to reduce energy costs while maintaining adequate ventilation. Ducted fume hoods are designed to evacuate hazardous contaminants effectively. To minimize ventilation costs, variable air volume (VAV) systems are often used. These systems adjust the volume of air exhausted based on the position of the sash, reducing energy consumption when the hood is not in active use. Automatic sash-closing devices further enhance energy efficiency by ensuring the hood operates at minimal exhaust volume when unattended. Given that a six-foot constant volume hood can consume as much energy as three average American homes, these measures significantly reduce energy costs and infrastructure strain. Advantages of Ducted Fume Hoods Fumes are completely removed from the workspace. Low maintenance requirements. Quiet operation, as the extract fan is located away from the operator. Disadvantages of Ducted Fume Hoods Ductwork can be visually unappealing. Heated air is removed from the workspace, increasing energy costs. Fumes are released into the atmosphere without treatment. Specific Types of Fume Hoods Low Flow/High Performance Recent advancements have led to the development of energy-efficient low-flow/high-performance fume hoods. These models maintain or improve operator protection while reducing HVAC operating costs. Perchloric Acid Fume Hoods These units include a water wash system within the ductwork. Perchloric acid fumes can settle and form explosive crystals, making it essential to clean the ductwork internally using a series of water sprays. Water Wash Fume Hoods These hoods feature an internal wash system that cleans the interior surfaces to prevent the accumulation of hazardous chemicals. Scrubber Fume Hoods Scrubber hoods absorb fumes through a chamber filled with plastic shapes that are sprayed with water. The chemicals are washed into a sump, often containing a neutralizing liquid, before the fumes are dispersed or disposed of conventionally. Usage Guidelines To determine whether a chemical requires a fume hood, consult its Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS). If in doubt, always use a fume hood. A new fume hood should come with an operating and maintenance manual detailing proper usage instructions. Before using a hood, ensure it is unoccupied and free of leftover materials. Gather all necessary reagents and equipment, and turn on the internal light if visibility is poor. Adjust the glass sash to a height that allows comfortable access while maintaining safety. Control Panels Most fume hoods are equipped with mains-powered control panels that perform functions such as: Warning of low airflow. Alerting users if the sash is raised too high, causing unsafe air velocity. Switching the extract fan on or off. Controlling the internal light. Additional features, such as switches for water wash systems, can also be included. Safety Warning Even with a properly functioning fume hood, users should never directly smell chemicals, as this can cause severe damage to the respiratory system. A safer method is to waft small amounts of the substance toward the nose using the palm, though this still carries risks if toxic fumes are present.
